source: Due South Outfitters + Fly Life Outdoors

conditions.overall: High Country streams running cool with clear to slightly stained water. Late spring conditions favor subsurface patterns and emerging aquatic insects.

top_flies.name: Pheasant Tail Nymph
top_flies.note: Dead-drift subsurface in pocket water; primary pattern for cooler, clear streams

top_flies.name: Elk Hair Caddis
top_flies.note: Dry fly during afternoon emergences; fish fast water and riffles

top_flies.name: Woolly Bugger
top_flies.note: Streamer pattern for deeper pools and overhanging banks; strip or dead-drift

top_flies.name: Blue-Winged Olive
top_flies.note: Small nymph and dry; reliable in cool, high-elevation conditions

top_flies.name: Stimulator
top_flies.note: Attractor dry for pocket water; high visibility in clear conditions

top_flies.name: Sulfur Nymph
top_flies.note: Yellow-brown subsurface pattern for late-spring conditions

tactics: Focus on dead-drift nymphing in pocket water and behind rocks; High Country elevation delays hatches 1-2 weeks vs. lower WNC
Fish early morning and late afternoon when water is coolest; avoid midday high sun
Target deeper pools and undercut banks where fish retreat in cooler water
Use light leaders (4-5x) and small nymphs (#14-18) in clear water; sight-fish when possible
Strip streamers slowly through deep holes and along woody cover; fish move less in cool conditions
Watch for afternoon caddis emergences on riffles; be ready with dry patterns by 2-4 PM

waters.name: North Fork New River (Ashe/Watauga)
waters.note: Primary High Country tailwater; steady flows, clear water, good holding structure in pocket water

waters.name: South Fork New River
waters.note: Productive in spring; cooler than main stem, supports good nymph fishing

waters.name: Watauga River
waters.note: High-elevation tributary; clear water, cool temperatures favor subsurface presentations

waters.name: Wilson Creek (Avery)
waters.note: Fast, rocky stream with good pocket water; ideal for dry fly and nymph combinations

elevation_note: High Country streams (Boone, 3300-4000ft) run 1-2 weeks behind lower-elevation WNC. Spring mayfly and caddis emergences typically lag by 10-14 days. Water temps remain cold; fish subsurface patterns aggressively.
